newsitem.title: INDIA: India working hard to stamp out child labour - ILO.
newsitem.headline: India working hard to stamp out child labour - ILO.

text.p: India, home to the world's largest child workforce, has taken unprecedented steps toward eradicating child labour but must ensure employers cooperate, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) said on Wednesday.
"That is the challenge facing the government," Mitsuko Horiuchi, ILO regional director for Asia and the Pacific, told a news conference.

Horiuchi applauded a Supreme Court move to crack down on the problem, apparently referring to a directive issued last December asking the government to identify and immediately release all child labourers employed in hazardous industries.
"India is perhaps the only country of the world which has passed such a judgement," she said.
India officially prohibited the employment of children under 14 in 1948 and in 1986 banned child labour in 17 industries considered hazardous.

Still the Labour Ministry says some 18 million children work instead of going to primary and secondary school, and children's rights activists say there are more than 55 million working in labour-intensive industries like match-making, quarrying, tanning, firework manufacturing and carpet-weaving.

Child labour activist Kailash Satyarthi said the Supreme Court had ordered employers of child slaves to pay a fine of 20,000 rupees ($560) per child, which would go towards rehabilitating the labourer.
Indian officials say their aim is to totally eradicate child labour by the year 2020, but have started by first targeting harmful industries because the problem is so pervasive.

Horiuchi said the ILO was thinking of reaching out to mothers rather than children in campaigning against child labour. "Otherwise it is a perpetual poverty cycle which goes on and on for generations," she said.
About 80 percent of India's child labourers work on farms and in roadside tea stalls, many to help repay their parents' debts to rural loan sharks.
